Issued at 247 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Elevated fire danger continues this afternoon with southwesterly 
winds gusting to 25-40 mph while humidity levels have fallen to 25-
35%. More details about the fire danger can be found in the fire 
weather discussion below. Highs have warmed to the 80s with a few 
locations breaking into the low 90s. These warm temperatures have 
warmed to near record highs for today. Could see a few records 
broken before temperatures begin cooling this evening. Should see 
winds remain steady to slowly weakening for the rest of the 
afternoon hours before more noticeably weakening this evening after 
sunset. Humidity will be increasing during this period of time as 
well, putting an end to the fire danger threat for today. However, a 
tighter surface pressure gradient (SPG) will remain in place through 
the night. This will keep elevated southerly winds through the 
night, resulting in another mild night with lows only falling to the 
60s. These temperatures will again be near record warm low 
territory. 

Sunday will be a much nicer day as low level pressure gradients 
relax across the area. There will still be marginally breezy 
southerly winds with gusts up to 20-25 mph. High temperatures will 
remain warm in the low to mid 80s thanks to the the thermal ridge 
axis sitting overhead. A cold front will be beginning to push into 
the area from the west. Thankfully, this front will deliver 
noticeably colder temperatures with overnight lows falling down to 
the 50s and 60s.

The front looks to push through the forecast area on Monday, leading 
to slightly cooler temperatures, but still above average highs in 
the upper 60s, 70s, and 80s. The coolest temperatures will reside in 
the northwest part of the forecast area. A weak mid level wave will 
pass through the area behind the surface cold front. There may be 
just enough moisture to squeak out some light showers along and 
north of highway-14. The ensembles show a broad 50-90% chance for 
rainfall totals to exceed a hundredth of an inch. Their 
probabilities quickly diminish to near zero for amounts to exceed a 
tenth of an inch. Rainfall chances (15-30%) will be highest during 
the daylight hours.

Tuesday looks to be a dry day as upper level ridging slightly 
strengthens ahead of a deepening upper level low over the southwest 
CONUS. Withe the previously mentioned cold front through the 
forecast area, highs will be closer to seasonable in the 60s to low 
70s.

Chances for rain begin to return to the area on Wednesday as the 
previously mentioned upper level low begins to eject into the 
Plains. However, medium range guidance continues to show a large 
variance in how this upper wave will evolve. Some show the wave 
continuing to push eastwards while others show a closed low 
developing and cutting off the mean flow. The ensembles also reflect 
these possibilities as well with the GFS ensembles having the wave 
continue to push into the Plains while the Euro and Canadian 
ensembles show a cut off low developing. Each of these models 
respective machine learning (ML) counterparts also show the same 
evolution. Looking to the clusters shows that the most favored 
cluster has the upper low closing off and detaching from the mean 
flow aloft. That said, the most favored cluster has this closed low 
just northeast of the four corners area and bringing increasing 
chances for rain to the forecast area. While this does look to be a 
more favorable solution, did not want to stray from the NBM's PoPs 
(30-60% chance) at this time as changes in the upper level patterns 
evolution remains possible. That said, the potential for rain and 
associated cloud cover looks to keep temperatures near seasonable in 
the 60s for Wednesday and Thursday. Friday looks to be the coolest 
day as broader troughing may encompass the Northern Plains. Should 
this play out, then highs may fall to near to below average in the 
50s.
